intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that annular epidermolytic ichthyosis-1 (AEI1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding keratin 10 (KRT10).

checks.evidence_quote: Molecular analysis revealed a novel tandem CG to GA 2-bp mutation in the same allele of keratin 10 in affected individuals
checks.explanation: The mutation is on one KRT10 allele in a disorder the paper says is autosomal dominant, so it is heterozygous.

paragraphs.text: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a rare variant of bullous congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, also called epidermolytic ichthyosis. Patients have bullous ichthyosis in early life. Later they develop hyperkeratotic plaques in the flexures and on extensor surfaces, along with intermittent episodes of annular and polycyclic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs. Skin biopsy shows epidermolytic hyperkeratosis (Joh et al., 1997; Suga et al., 1998; Mikilita et al., 2020).

checks.evidence_quote: Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis (AEI) is a rare phenotypic variant of epidermolytic ichthyosis (EI), also known as congenital bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma

paragraphs.text: Sahn et al. (1992) described a 30-year-old white woman who developed bullous and ichthyosiform skin lesions at age 8 months. The blistering stopped at puberty, but hyperkeratotic plaques persisted. At age 27 years she developed many annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and limbs. These plaques were itchy, slowly enlarged, and then resolved. Biopsy of the annular plaques showed epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. On electron microscopy there were interrupted perinuclear tonofilament rings, consistent with either bullous ichthyotic erythroderma of Brocq or ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens. Two of her 5 children had a bullous type of ichthyosis. In a literature review, Mikilita et al. (2020) noted that this woman also had mild palmoplantar keratoderma with fissures. Her 2-year-old son had developed papules at age 6 months that progressed to blisters and crusts, and he later had keratotic plaques on the neck and in the armpits.

paragraphs.text: Joh et al. (1997) reported a family with affected members in 2 generations. The proband had bullous ichthyosis and episodes of disease activity marked by many annular and polycyclic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs. Histology showed the typical changes of epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Ultrastructural analysis showed abnormal keratin filament networks and perinuclear clumping of tonofilaments. As summarized by Mikilita et al. (2020), the affected members were a father and his daughter. The father had widespread blisters from birth. From his first year until age 16 years he had intermittent, itchy, hyperkeratotic, erythematous plaques with blisters. At age 31 years he again had intermittent blisters and hyperkeratotic plaques, together with annular, migratory, polycyclic, scaly, erythematous plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs. His daughter had generalized bullous lesions and moderate erythema from her second day of life.

paragraphs.text: Suga et al. (1998) described a third kindred with annular epidermolytic ichthyosis. The proband was an 11-year-old boy, and his mother and sister were also affected. They noted that people with this variant have bullous ichthyosis in early childhood and later develop hyperkeratotic, lichenified plaques in the flexures and on extensor surfaces, as well as intermittent bouts of annular and polycyclic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs. In their review, Mikilita et al. (2020) noted that the proband had no history of blisters. He had xerotic plaques in the flexures and on extensor surfaces from age 7 months, and at age 11 years he had intermittent annular, erythematous, scaly, serpiginous plaques.

paragraphs.text: Mikilita et al. (2020) reported an 8-year-old Brazilian girl with skin disease that began in the first months of life. Her parents were not consanguineous, and no other family members were affected. On examination she had erythematous, scaly, hyperkeratotic plaques with prominent borders on the mesogastrium, cubital and popliteal fossae, groin, and neck. She also had palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and yellowish hyperkeratotic plaques on the scalp and nasal introitus. Hair, nails, and mucosa were normal. One month later the affected area had grown, but the polycyclic pattern had disappeared. Biopsy of the forearm showed acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis with marked epidermolysis of the granular layer. The initial working diagnosis had been erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva. Mikilita et al. (2020) also reviewed 19 previously reported cases from 10 publications.

paragraphs.text: In their review of reported cases, Mikilita et al. (2020) found that topical treatments gave little benefit. These included retinoids, corticosteroids, propylene glycol, calcipotriene, and keratolytic agents. Systemic retinoids gave a good response in some patients: oral acitretin (20 mg per day in the father reported by Joh et al. (1997)) and low-dose oral isotretinoin. One mother and son did not improve with etretinate.
